title: The Surge Trigger
primary_metric: total expected cost of a mobile-unit redeployment trigger design (Option A's flat verification-protocol cost vs. Option B's late-detection cost, sized by the gap in that day's new-case count between the two trigger days); lower cost wins

options.A: The True-Curve Trigger -- redeploy the moment the modeled true-infection curve I(t)'s growth rate I'(t) crosses threshold, found via the chain rule
options.B: The Reported-Curve Trigger -- redeploy only once the observable reported-case curve D(t)'s growth rate D'(t) crosses its own threshold, found via the product rule

deliverables.text: The true-infection model I(t) from Appendix A, differentiated using the chain rule to find I'(t) (shown step by step, naming the outer and inner functions), the exact day t_A where I'(t) first equals Appendix D's True-Curve threshold, and the equation of the tangent line to I(t) at t = t_A.

The reported-case model D(t) = I(t) x c(t) from Appendices A and C, differentiated using the product rule to find D'(t) (shown step by step, naming both factors and their own derivatives), and the exact day t_B where D'(t) first equals Appendix D's Reported-Curve threshold.

A classification of D(t)'s one critical point in this window as a local maximum (using D'(t) from D2 and a sign argument or equivalent reasoning), the day it occurs and D(t)'s value there, and a written comparison to I(t)'s behavior over the same window -- specifically, whether I(t) has any turning point of its own in this window, and what that difference means for anyone who assumes the reported curve peaking means the true outbreak is peaking.

A quotient-rule derivation of R(t) = D(t) / I(t), shown step by step with the full (D'I - DI')/I^2 setup before any simplification, verifying algebraically that R(t) reduces exactly to Appendix C's capture-rate model c(t) -- then, using t_A (D1) and t_B (D2), the resulting lag in days, the resulting gap in that day's new-case count between the two trigger days, and a total-expected-cost calculation for each trigger design using Appendix D's cost figures, shown step by step for both options.

A one-paragraph written recommendation that names which trigger design has the lower total expected cost and explicitly addresses why assuming the reported curve is "the same outbreak, just a delayed copy" of the true curve -- rather than a curve with its own, genuinely different shape -- would have been misleading, citing D3's finding directly.

balance.argument_a: Option A (The True-Curve Trigger) is the earliest-possible warning: it fires at t_A = 10.41 days, the moment the modeled true-infection curve's own growth rate crosses 1.00 new cases/day per day, found by the chain rule directly on Appendix A's exponential model. Its cost is fixed and known in advance -- the department's own $1,700.00 verification-protocol cost [MA5], charged flat regardless of outcome, because policy requires paying it before acting on any unconfirmed model. A's real strength is certainty: no matter how the outbreak actually unfolds, A's total cost never changes.
balance.argument_b: Option B (The Reported-Curve Trigger) waits for the only curve the department can actually observe -- D(t) = I(t) x c(t) -- to cross its own 0.40 threshold, which happens at t_B = 14.43 days, found by the product rule. Under this case's own numbers B is the cheaper design overall: the roughly 4.03-day lag against A costs a real, computed $1,527.92 in late-detection cost (the gap in that day's new-case count, priced via Appendix D's [S4] figure), which is less than A's flat $1,700.00 verification cost. B's real case is that A's verification cost is a real, certain expense paid for a signal the department has chosen never to trust outright -- while B's cost, though real, is smaller under the case's disclosed assumptions.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |cost(loser) - cost(winner)| / cost(loser) x 100 (the corpus's standard margin formula, dividing by the LOSING option's cost -- per skills/case-readiness/scripts/tier2_probes.py's probe_sensitivity, which this case's sensitivity_model.py matches exactly once its higher-wins sign convention is unwound). t_A solves I0*k*e^(k*t_A) = threshold_A (chain rule derivative); t_B solves I0*e^(k*t_B)*(k*(c0-m*t_B)-m) = threshold_B (product rule derivative), on the rising branch before D(t)'s own local maximum at t=32.695. cost(A) = verification_cost = $1,700.00 (MA5) (loser, higher cost). cost(B) = (I(t_B)-I(t_A)) x cost_per_case = 4.897 x $312.00 = $1,527.92 (winner, lower cost). margin = |$1,700.00 - $1,527.92| / $1,700.00 x 100 = $172.08 / $1,700.00 x 100 = 10.12%. This is within the approved concept's 8-15% margin target. NOTE: I0 (MA1), the capture-rate pair c0/m (MA3), and the flat verification cost (MA5) are stated Modeling Assumptions, not sourced figures; the growth constant k (MA2) is directly informed by a real, sourced early-outbreak doubling-time figure [S1] but is itself a stated assumption for this fictional county; only the $312.00 per-case figure [S4] is a real, sourced value used directly. This margin is a designed property of the chosen assumption values, not an empirical finding.
